title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol

hero.subtitle: The original specification for email delivery that established how messages traverse the Internet, still in use (updated) over 40 years later.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) defines the mechanism for transmitting email messages between mail servers. It operates on a store-and-forward model where messages are relayed between Mail Transfer Agents (MTAs).

Jon Postel authored this RFC along with many other foundational Internet standards. SMTP remains one of the oldest protocols still in active daily use, handling billions of emails per day.
sections.plainLanguage: The Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) defines how email messages move between mail servers. It works by store and forward: Mail Transfer Agents relay each message from one server to the next. SMTP is one of the oldest protocols still used every day.

sections.title: SMTP Commands
sections.content:
SMTP uses a simple text-based command-response protocol over TCP port 25.

HELOIdentify the sending host
MAIL FROMSpecify the envelope sender
RCPT TOSpecify an envelope recipient
DATABegin the message body
QUITClose the connection
RSETReset the session state
NOOPNo operation; the receiver just replies OK
VRFYVerify a mailbox exists
sections.plainLanguage: SMTP is a text-based command and reply protocol over TCP port 25. Key commands are HELO (identify the sending host), MAIL FROM (the sender), RCPT TO (a recipient), DATA (start the message body) and QUIT (close the connection).

sections.title: Reply Codes
sections.content:
SMTP reply codes are three-digit numbers where the first digit indicates the class of response:

2xxPositive completion (e.g., 250 OK)
3xxPositive intermediate (e.g., 354 Start mail input)
4xxTransient negative (e.g., 451 Local error)
5xxPermanent negative (e.g., 550 Mailbox unavailable)
sections.plainLanguage: Every SMTP reply is a three-digit code whose first digit gives the class. 2xx means success, 3xx means more input is needed, 4xx means a temporary failure to retry later, and 5xx means a permanent failure.

sections.title: Legacy and Evolution
sections.content:
RFC 821 was replaced by RFC 2821 and then RFC 5321, which add the EHLO greeting and service extensions. Later separate extension documents added STARTTLS, authentication, and internationalized email. The core store-and-forward model remains unchanged.

ESMTP
Extended SMTP (RFC 2821, RFC 5321) adds capability negotiation via EHLO
STARTTLS
Opportunistic encryption for SMTP connections
SPF/DKIM/DMARC
Authentication mechanisms to prevent email spoofing
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 821 was replaced by RFC 2821 and then RFC 5321, which add the EHLO greeting and extensions. Later documents added STARTTLS for encryption and authentication, and SPF, DKIM and DMARC help prevent spoofing. The core store-and-forward model is unchanged.

subtitle: The original specification for email delivery, still in use (updated) over 40 years later
summary: SMTP is a simple, text-based protocol for moving mail between hosts. A sending program opens a connection, names the sender with MAIL and each recipient with RCPT, sends the message after DATA, and each step is answered with a three-digit reply code. Mail can be relayed through intermediate hosts. This 1982 version was replaced by RFC 2821 and then RFC 5321.

plainLanguage.summary: SMTP is a simple text protocol for moving mail between hosts. The sender names itself with MAIL and each recipient with RCPT, then sends the message after DATA. Every step gets a three-digit reply code. Mail can be relayed through intermediate hosts. RFC 5321 replaced this 1982 version.

tldr.problem: Hosts on different networks needed one agreed way to hand mail from the sender's machine to the recipient's machine reliably.
tldr.mechanism: The sender opens a TCP connection to the receiver and sends short text commands (HELO, MAIL, RCPT, DATA, QUIT); the receiver answers each with a three-digit reply code.
tldr.outcome: One lock-step dialog moves a message, possibly via relays, and the same model is still how Internet mail travels.

facts.label: Core commands
facts.value: HELO, MAIL, RCPT, DATA, RSET, QUIT

today: RFC 821 itself has been replaced twice, but the dialog it defined is still recognizable in current mail servers: connect, greet, MAIL, RCPT, DATA, QUIT. Modern SMTP adds EHLO extensions, STARTTLS encryption, authentication and internationalized addresses, and uses SPF, DKIM and DMARC to fight forged senders.
